newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE - 2-yr yield sinks, Fed seen steady.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE - 2-yr yield sinks, Fed seen steady.

text.p: A dramatic decline in U.S. Treasury yields this week suggested the bond market is growing more confident the Federal Reserve might leave monetary policy unchanged through the summer, Wall Street players said.
"The market has clearly taken out expectations of a Fed tightening in July and August," said Scott Graham, co-head trader at Prudential Securities Inc.
Analysts said a sharp drop in the two-year note yield on Friday morning was one indication the market appears confident the Fed will stand pat on monetary policy for a while.

The two-year note yield fell to 5.99 percent Friday morning, its first time below the six-percent level since late February. It not only smashed its 6.10 percent resistence level, it also broke through its 15-week moving average of 6.15 percent and its 200-day average of 6.06 percent.
"This is big!" said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market analyst at UBS Securities LLC.

"No one is talking about a (Fed) ease, but when you trade inside of 50 basis points (on the spread between the two-year note and Fed funds) you have to say the direction of the next Fed move is unknown," he added.
The spread between the two-year note and the current federal funds rate of 5.50 percent narrowed to 49 basis points Friday from 58 basis points Thursday and 68 Wednesday.

Typically, a spread of 75 to 100 basis points suggests the market anticipates a tightening; 50 to 75 basis indicates a steady Fed; a spread significantly below 50 basis points would point to an easing.

Sparking the narrowing of the two-year note/federal funds spread was a 0.3 percent drop in the May producer price index. The PPI's fifth straight monthly decline followed a weaker-than-expected May retail sales report on Thursday.

Consequently, Treasury yields fell to their lowest levels since February 25 -- a day before Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan spooked the market in what was perceived at the time as a hawkish Humphrey Hawkins testimony.
"It was Greenspan who forced us to think about rate hikes," Dimick said, recalling the testimony.
Along with the 18-basis-point fall in the two-year note yield the past two sessions, the 30-year cash bond yield fell to 6.72 percent on Friday, from 6.78 on Thursday and 6.84 percent on Wednesday.
"There was so much cash on the sidelines that a lot of towels were being thrown in," Graham said. "And when you throw in the towel, it's a feeding frenzy."
Analysts explained that the market's action is more about the excellent technical factors than fundamentals.
Those who had set up short positions, anticipating stronger data, were forced to cover those positions to cut their losses when the market started to go up.
Jim Nealis, head bond trader at PaineWebber Inc, said now that the two-year fell below 6 percent, people will likely start ignoring the short end.
"The story is now intermediates," he said. "The front end is not the story anymore.
He said that with a combination of good technical and fundamental factors supporting the market, players are extending out the curve to five-, 10-, and 30-year securities for duration.
"A lot of curve flattening trades are coming off," Prudential's Graham said.
"With the Fed out of the picture those negative carry trades were eating away ot the cost base," he added.
But the rally, led by the short end, is likely to end soon, with analysts forseeing a decline of perhaps just another five basis points across the yield curve.

"There is a sense that the market is trading a bit rich relative to the reality of the situation," Dimick said, adding that despite the consumer spending slowdown in the second quarter, "there is every reason to believe the consumer is alive and well.

"Until we see evidence of a recovery in spending, which might not be until the first week in July ... the market will trade sideways to slightly higher," he said. "We can run further, not because people think the Fed will ease, but because people will be forced to cover (shorts) against their will."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
